newsitem.title: USA: US court lifts injunction on Stockpile cobalt sale.
newsitem.headline: US court lifts injunction on Stockpile cobalt sale.

text.p: The Defense National Stockpile Center said the U.S. Court of Federal Claims has lifted its injunction on sealed bid cobalt sales, thus opening the way to a resumption of offers to the market.
Stockpile administrator Richard Connelly said no decision has been taken yet on when the first sale will take place, but it was likely to be a sealed, rather than negotiated sale.
Stockpile normally gives 30 days notice before an offer of metal is made to the market, Connelly said, adding that the summer was not usually a good time to sell material.
In an order dated June 18 Judge Tidwell of the U.S. Court of Federal Claims reaffirmed Stockpile's authority to prohibit the submission of "all or none" offers, Stockpile said in a statement.

Connelly told Reuters the domestic preference clause, which prompted trader Minor Metals Inc to contest the March sealed bid 005 sale and obtain the injunction, will not be included in the next sealed bid sale. The March sale, initially suspended, will now be cancelled, he added.
Stockpile had suspended all cobalt sales, negotiated and sealed, until the legal tangle with Minor Metals was cleared.
The suspension had helped to push up cobalt prices in recent weeks before softening again.
Connelly said the "all or none" provision in Stockpile offers for metal will continue.
Officials at Minor Metals or their attorneys were not immediately available for comment.

Judge Tidwell ruled last month that Stockpile had the authority to include domestic preference clauses in sealed bid sales, but was unhappy with how it was enforced and asked Stockpile to look at this issue.
Stockpile filed further information to the court enabling Tidwell to reach his final ruling which lifted the injuction.

In another, separate case involving Stockpile cobalt sales and Minor Metals in the U.S. District Court, Eastern District of Virginia, Connelly said he was confident the judge will reaffirm his decision to throw out a complaint filed by the trading company.
Minor Metals has asked the court to review its decision.
Connelly said although Stockpile has the right to offer all the cobalt it has left in the little time remaining in its current fiscal year which ends September 30, it was unlikely to do so.
"I would not do that - I think it would be a bit much. The market would not be able to soak up that much at one time," Connelly said.
Stockpile will have authority to sell 6 million lbs of cobalt in the next fiscal year and will not be allowed to carry over any unsold material from the current year.
